samples.summary: CLI-mode OAuth entry (`?mode=cli`) still has no browser-side CSRF binding, while the same guard now adds one for the web branch — a cross-site-initiated navigation can make a victim's browser emit a valid Wafflebase auth code to an attacker-chosen loopback port
samples.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` splits at `if (mode !== 'cli')` (github-auth.guard.ts:67). The web branch mints a random state AND mirrors it into `wafflebase_oauth_state` so the callback can prove the browser started the login (github-auth.guard.ts:75-81, verified at auth.controller.ts:250-267). The CLI branch (github-auth.guard.ts:85-101) mints only a server-side state entry and sets no cookie, and `githubAuthCallback` skips `consumeWebOAuthState` entirely whenever `cliState?.mode === 'cli'` (auth.controller.ts:126-128). `GET /auth/github` is unauthenticated and reachable by top-level navigation. Attack: a hostile page navigates the victim to `https://api.example/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker-picked 1024-65535>&nonce=<attacker nonce>`; GitHub silently re-approves the already-authorized app; the callback mints a CLI code for the VICTIM's account and 302s the victim's browser to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<victim code>&nonce=<attacker nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:143-157). The 60s single-use code is now in the victim's browser history and in the request log/URL of whatever local service listens on that port. The nonce added by this change does not defend here because the attacker supplies it. The port range check (1024-65535) is the only limit on the target. This is pre-existing behaviour that the change relocated/renamed rather than introduced, but the change is precisely the one that adds a browser binding to the sibling branch and leaves this one without.

samples.summary: The DNS-rebinding pin protecting the new SSRF gate is silently dropped for every hop whenever an egress proxy env var is set, so the gate's verdict and the connect-time resolution diverge
samples.evidence: `hopDispatcher` returns `new ProxyAgent(proxy)` and never `pinnedAgent(addresses)` when `proxyForUrl(target)` finds `http_proxy`/`https_proxy`/`all_proxy` (image-fetcher.ts:483-495). Since `proxyForUrl` reads `process.env` by default (image-fetcher.ts:542-559), merely exporting `all_proxy` disables the address pin for all attacker-influenced document image `src` values. A ~0s-TTL nameserver can then answer `assertFetchableImageUrl`'s lookup publicly and the proxy's lookup with an internal address, reaching the proxy's network. The code and `docs/design/cli.md` both state this explicitly as an accepted residual risk with a rationale (proxy protocols carry a name, not an address), so this is recorded rather than hidden — flagging so the acceptance is a reviewed decision rather than an implicit one.

samples.summary: The login nonce — the sole binding for the loopback callback — is written to stderr and passed as a process argument, so any co-resident user or captured transcript can complete the pending login
samples.evidence: `const oauthUrl = `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}&nonce=${encodeURIComponent(nonce)}`` is printed via `console.error` (login.ts:246-247) and then handed to `deps.openBrowser(oauthUrl)` (login.ts:253), which spawns `open` with the URL in argv — readable by any local user via `ps`. Anyone who reads it and can reach `127.0.0.1:<port>` within the 30s listener lifetime can replay a callback of their own choosing, defeating `nonceMatches` (login.ts:320-325). The code comment and `docs/design/cli.md` acknowledge this; the printed fallback is deliberate because `open()` cannot report whether a browser appeared. Reported so the trade-off is explicit.

samples.summary: `--allow-unbound-callback` fully disables the loopback callback nonce binding, restoring the login-fixation vector the nonce exists to close
samples.evidence: `if (nonce === null && allowUnbound) { console.error('Accepting a callback with no login nonce...') }` (login.ts:399-402) accepts any nonce-less `/callback?code=` while the flag is set. Because the listener is reachable by any local process and by any web page that guesses the port, an attacker who wins the race can seat the operator inside the attacker's account. The mitigation is that the flag is opt-in, warned on stderr (login.ts:227-231), documented only in `--help`/README (never surfaced by an attacker-triggerable diagnostic — the timeout message is deliberately invariant at login.ts:478-483), and a *mismatched* nonce is still refused. This is a sound design; flagged so the downgrade surface is on the record.

samples.summary: The backend serves `?mode=cli` logins that carry no nonce, minting a state whose loopback redirect carries no binding at all
samples.evidence: `if (raw === undefined) { this.logger.warn(...) }` (github-auth.guard.ts:91-94) leaves `nonce` undefined, and `auth.controller.ts:152-154` then omits `&nonce=` from the loopback redirect. Any unauthenticated party can therefore drive the flow to produce an unbound loopback callback. The stated rationale (published npm CLIs would break; an attacker minting a code for a port they control simply picks their own nonce, so a server-side requirement buys nothing) is correct — a current CLI always sends a nonce and refuses a nonce-less callback (login.ts:403-410), so no current client is downgraded. Reported as a hardening item to close once old CLIs are out of support, as the doc says.

samples.summary: The new OAuth state cookie inherits `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'`, so a self-hosted deploy that does not set NODE_ENV ships the CSRF-binding cookie without the Secure flag
samples.evidence: `baseCookieOptions()` returns `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` (cookies.ts:29-35) and is now the single definition shared by the session cookies and the new `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie (auth.controller.ts:311-316, github-auth.guard.ts:77-80). A deployment behind TLS but with NODE_ENV unset (a common self-hosted mistake) exposes the state cookie — and the session cookies — to network-position stripping. Pre-existing pattern now extended to a security-critical cookie; a TLS-derived or explicitly-configured flag would be safer.

samples.summary: The web OAuth state cookie uses one fixed name with no per-flow scoping, so any cross-site-initiated `/auth/github` navigation overwrites an in-flight login's state
samples.evidence: `res.cookie(OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE_NAME, state, {...})` (github-auth.guard.ts:77-80) always writes the same cookie name. A hostile page (or a second tab) that causes the victim's browser to hit `/auth/github` replaces the pending state, and `consumeWebOAuthState` then rejects the genuine callback with a 400 (auth.controller.ts:258-266). Attacker-triggerable login denial only — the attacker cannot learn or choose the value, so it is not a fixation vector.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo. GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate branches at github-auth.guard.ts:67; the web branch mints a random state and mirrors it into the OAUTH_STATE cookie (github-auth.guard.ts:75-81), which auth.controller.ts:250-267 enforces. The CLI branch (github-auth.guard.ts:85-101) validates only the port range and optional nonce shape and creates a server-side state entry with no cookie, and auth.controller.ts:126-128 skips consumeWebOAuthState whenever cliState.mode === 'cli'. GET /auth/github (auth.controller.ts:96-97) is unauthenticated and reachable by cross-site top-level navigation with attacker-controlled mode/port/nonce. On callback, auth.controller.ts:143-157 mints a code for the victim's account (cli-auth.store.ts:62-67) and 302s the victim's browser to http://127.0.0.1:<attacker port>/callback?code=...&nonce=<attacker nonce>; that code is exchangeable for access+refresh tokens at the unauthenticated POST /auth/cli/exchange (auth.controller.ts:167-183). The CLI-side nonce check (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:398-410) only protects a legitimately running CLI from a foreign callback; it does not prevent the server from emitting a victim-scoped code to an attacker-chosen loopback port, because the attacker supplies the nonce. No guard elsewhere blocks the path; the guard's own comment (github-auth.guard.ts:26-42) documents the missing browser binding as intentional rather than mitigated. In-lane (OAuth CSRF / auth-code exposure) and real.

finding.summary: SSRF address pin is silently dropped whenever an egress proxy applies, re-opening DNS rebinding through the proxy's own resolution
finding.evidence: `hopDispatcher()` returns a `ProxyAgent` and never a `pinnedAgent` when `proxyForUrl(target)` matches (image-fetcher.ts:397-409). The file comment and `docs/design/cli.md` both claim "Dropping the pin there costs nothing that was ever held ... under a proxy the CLI performs no connect-time resolution at all." That is only half true: the proxy resolves the name instead, and its answer is not the answer the gate approved. Vector: an attacker who can edit/share a document sets `src=http://rebind.attacker/x` behind a nameserver with ~0s TTL. `assertFetchableImageUrl` (line 316) resolves it to a public address and allows it; the request is then handed to the operator's `http_proxy`, which re-resolves `rebind.attacker` and gets `169.254.169.254` (or an internal host). The proxy fetches it and the bytes are embedded in the PDF/DOCX/PPTX the victim reads — exactly the SSRF this gate exists to stop, on precisely the machines (corporate, proxy-only egress) where internal targets are most valuable. The gate's own resolution is not authoritative for the proxied hop, so nothing else constrains it. Mitigation would be to pass the gate's approved address as the connect target (or refuse to proxy names whose gate-time and request-time identity cannot be tied), rather than asserting the risk is nil.

verdict.reason: The core technical claim is present and unguarded. hopDispatcher (packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:479-496) returns a ProxyAgent whenever proxyForUrl(target) matches (483-486) and only reaches pinnedAgent(addresses) on the no-proxy path (495). proxyForUrl (542-559) reads http_proxy/https_proxy/all_proxy from the ambient env, so on proxy-only hosts every http(s) hop is un-pinned. The fetch loop (666-681) computes the gate's approved addresses via assertFetchableImageUrl (321-409) and then discards them on the proxied path; the proxy performs its own connect-time resolution, so a ~0s-TTL rebinding host can answer the gate with a public address (394-400) and the proxy with an internal one, and the bytes land in the exported document. I searched for any compensating check and found none — isInternalHostname (385) only screens the name/literal, and pinnedAgent (422-444) is never applied to a proxied hop. The reviewer's quoted comment text is inaccurate: lines 462-472 and docs/design/cli.md:944-957 explicitly state the residual risk is real and accepted rather than nil. But a documented, deliberately accepted risk is not a refutation ground, and the vector itself (SSRF into the proxy's network reachable by any attacker who can set an image src in a shared document) is squarely in the security lane and matches the code. No named refutation ground applies.

finding.summary: Web GitHub OAuth flow forwards no `state`, and passport does not validate one — OAuth login-CSRF / session fixation on the browser path; the `csrf` token CliAuthStore mints is never verified anywhere
finding.evidence: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` sets `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` is present (github.strategy.ts:59-62), i.e. only for `mode=cli`. The constructor `super({...})` (lines 43-49) passes no `state: true` and no `store`, so passport-oauth2 installs a `NullStore` whose `verify` always succeeds — no state is generated, sent, or checked for the ordinary web login. `AuthController.githubAuthCallback` then reaches the web branch with `stateToken === undefined` and unconditionally sets session cookies (auth.controller.ts:145-149). Vector: attacker starts GitHub OAuth for their own account, captures the resulting `?code=`, and makes the victim's browser load `GET /auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>`; the backend mints and sets `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` cookies for the attacker's account, so the victim silently works inside the attacker's account (classic OAuth login CSRF / session fixation). `CliAuthStore.createState` generates a per-request `csrf` (cli-auth.store.ts:32) and `consumeState` returns it (line 55), but a repo-wide grep for `csrf` finds no consumer outside the store and its own specs — the intended control was never wired up. Pre-existing rather than introduced here, but this change is the one hardening this exact flow and the diff's own design-doc table claims "OAuth state forgery (CSRF)" is mitigated.

verdict.reason: The finding claims the web GitHub OAuth flow forwards and validates no `state`, and that the callback unconditionally sets session cookies. Both are false in this working tree; the reviewer evidently read a stale revision (it cites `req.__cliStateToken`, an identifier that no longer exists — the current hand-off is `__oauthState`). Counterexample: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` takes the explicit `mode !== 'cli'` web branch (github-auth.guard.ts:67-83) and mints `randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')`, mirrors it into the httpOnly/SameSite=Lax `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie (github-auth.guard.ts:77-80, cookies.ts:16,29-35) and sets `req.__oauthState` (line 81). `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` forwards that value for every request, not just CLI (github.strategy.ts:59-66), and `/auth/github` is guarded by `GitHubAuthGuard` (auth.controller.ts:97), so every web authorization request carries a state. On the callback, `githubAuthCallback` calls `consumeWebOAuthState` whenever the state is not a CLI state (auth.controller.ts:123-128), BEFORE `findOrCreateUser` and before `setAuthCookies` (line 162); `consumeWebOAuthState` clears the cookie and throws `BadRequestException` unless the query `state` is present and constant-time-equal to the cookie (auth.controller.ts:250-267, using timingSafeEqualString at 39-43). The reviewer's exact vector — callback reached with `stateToken === undefined` — is rejected by the `!stateToken` branch at line 259-266, and an attacker cannot forge a matching state because it lives in the victim's httpOnly cookie. A CLI-mode state cannot reach the web branch either: `cliState?.mode === 'cli'` diverts to the loopback redirect (lines 143-158) without ever calling `setAuthCookies`. The residual accurate detail — `CliAuthStore.createState`'s `csrf` (cli-auth.store.ts:32,42,54) has no consumer outside the store and its specs — is unused dead code, not the binding: the web path is bound by the cookie and the CLI path by the server-side state entry plus the nonce echo, so it is not a blocking auth weakness.

finding.summary: Image-gate server exemption keys only on (port, resolved address), never on hostname, so any attacker-named host resolving to the API server's address on its port is fetched with an attacker-chosen path and Host header
finding.evidence: `mayBeServer` is true whenever `effectivePort(url) === effectivePort(server)` (line 307-308) and the `allowed` filter passes any address in `exempt` unconditionally — `exempt.has(a.toLowerCase()) || (!internalName && !isPrivateAddress(a))` (lines 322-325) — where `exempt` is the set of addresses the configured `--server` resolves to (`serverAddresses`, line 253). The hostname of the image URL is never compared to the server's. Vector: with the documented dev setup `--server http://localhost:3000` (exempt = {127.0.0.1}), a malicious document carries `src=http://evil.attacker.tld:3000/<any path>` whose A record is 127.0.0.1. The private-address check is skipped because the address is in `exempt`, and the CLI issues `GET /<any path>` to 127.0.0.1:3000 with `Host: evil.attacker.tld`, embedding the response bytes into the exported artifact. The same holds for a self-hosted `--server https://wafflebase.corp.internal` (exempt = its internal address), turning the exemption into an attacker-steerable reader of arbitrary paths on the internal API host — including any Host-routed vhost co-located on that address. Tightening to an origin/hostname match (or at least rejecting a name that is not the server's own) closes it without breaking the localhost/127.0.0.1 spelling case the exemption exists for.

verdict.reason: The code is not as described. `mayBeServer` is not `portMatches` alone: lines 377-379 require `portMatches && (sameName || loopbackPair || ipLiteral(url.hostname) !== null)`, where `sameName` is precisely the hostname comparison the finding claims is absent (`normalizeHost(url.hostname) === normalizeHost(server.hostname)`, lines 368-371) and `loopbackPair` uses the name-level `isLoopbackHost` (lines 230-235), which resolves only literals and RFC 6761 names, not a foreign name's A record. Tracing the finding's own vector — `--server http://localhost:3000`, `src=http://evil.attacker.tld:3000/path` with an A record of 127.0.0.1 — gives sameName=false, loopbackPair=false, ipLiteral=null, so mayBeServer=false, so `exempt` is the EMPTY set (lines 389-392 are gated on `mayBeServer`, not on port). The `allowed` filter (394-400) then falls to `!internalName && !isPrivateAddress(a)`, and isPrivateIPv4 returns true for a===127 (line 100), leaving `allowed` empty and throwing at 401-408 with no request issued. The self-hosted variant is closed too: an attacker name ending in .internal/.local is refused at line 386 (`internalName && !mayBeServer`), and a public name resolving to an RFC1918 internal address is refused by isPrivateAddress. The behavior is pinned by an existing test that encodes this exact attack (packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts:352-365, 'refuses a foreign name aimed at the server address and port'), plus the internal-name case at 367-376. The fix the finding recommends is already the implementation. The cited line numbers (307-308, 322-325) do not match this file, and grep found no other copy of the gate.

finding.summary: The login nonce — the only secret binding the loopback callback — is printed to stderr and passed as browser argv, so anyone who can read the CLI's logs during the 30s window can complete a login fixation
finding.evidence: `runLogin` generates the nonce (line 226) and then prints the full OAuth URL including it: `console.error(`Opening browser: ${oauthUrl}`)` (line 239), where `oauthUrl` embeds both `port` and `nonce` (line 238); it is also handed to `open()` as a process argument (line 197). Everything else in this change treats the nonce as a secret (constant-time compare, `403` on mismatch, `redactUrl` applied to every other URL that reaches stderr). Vector: an attacker who can read the CLI's stderr — a captured CI/agent transcript, a shared terminal recording, another process able to read the browser's cmdline — learns `<port>` and `<nonce>` while the 30s listener is still open, then completes `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>` as *themselves*; the backend echoes the victim's nonce (auth.controller.ts:130-135), the victim's CLI accepts the callback and writes a session for the attacker's account. `docs/tasks/active/20260803-cli-system-exit-code-lessons.md` acknowledges the nonce "does travel in the printed OAuth URL and the browser argv", but neither the CLI README nor `docs/design/cli.md` §8.1 records that the printed URL must be treated as a credential — the design doc presents the binding as unqualified. At minimum the printed URL deserves a "do not share while login is pending" note, and agent-facing capture of that line should be considered secret.

verdict.reason: The finding's stated defect is not present as described. It asserts the nonce-bearing URL is printed with no acknowledgement and that "at minimum the printed URL deserves a 'do not share while login is pending' note" and that neither the README nor docs/design/cli.md §8.1 records the URL as a credential. Both are false in this tree: login.ts:248-250 prints exactly that note ("Do not share it while this login is pending — it carries the nonce binding the callback to this terminal.") immediately after the URL, and login.ts:238-245 documents the tradeoff inline; docs/design/cli.md:975-984 states in bold "The printed OAuth URL is a credential while the login is pending," names the browser-argv and stderr-capture vectors explicitly, and bounds the exposure (loopback-only callback, 30s listener lifetime). The residual exposure is intrinsic to the loopback OAuth fallback — the URL must be printable because open() cannot report whether a browser actually appeared (login.ts:252-256) — and exploiting it requires the attacker to already reach 127.0.0.1 on the victim machine (srv.listen(0,'127.0.0.1') at login.ts:492) within timeoutMs 30_000 (login.ts:365). The nonce binding itself is enforced and intact: constant-time compare (login.ts:320-325) and non-settling 403 on missing/mismatched nonce (login.ts:398-410). Not a blocking security defect under the rubric.
